tasks.locator: eMethods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (begins p. 5; the model, covariate and interaction sentences on p. 6) (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/VickersSmith_2025_Supplement.pdf)
tasks.extracted: Each GEE model included baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, and, for each drug-use day, drug category, study week and part of the week; education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose entered the behaviour models only, and the daily composite score and the number of times strips were used entered the nonfatal overdose model only (the same sets as the article's Table 3 notes d and g; injecting is not a covariate in any model). Whether the association with the composite score and with nonfatal overdose was modified was tested by two-way interactions of baseline strip use with state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and study week, and, for overdose only, daily injection: seven modifiers for overdose and six for the composite score. A missing-at-random mixed model was fitted for the composite score only; all P values are called descriptive.

tasks.locator: eFigure 5 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/VickersSmith_2025_Supplement.pdf); publisher HTML: Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: eFigure 5 plots, for each group, the adjusted mean daily probability of a self-reported nonfatal overdose across the 28-day observation period against age, on a log scale; the article's Results say the association was modified by age in adjusted but not in unadjusted analyses, and give no age-specific ratios. Editors' reading of the figure (measured from the image): the probabilities are drawn with 95% bands over ages 19 to 76; the strip group's line falls steeply with age while the comparison group's stays nearly flat, the two crossing at about age 42, so the modelled risk is higher in the strip group among younger and lower among older participants; the two bands overlap at every age; the plotted probabilities (about 0.0003 to 0.014 in the strip group and 0.002 to 0.003 in the comparison group) are well below the mean daily risk of 0.02 in the article's Table 3, so they were computed at covariate values the figure does not state.

tasks.extracted: Supplemental Table 2, which the text cites for 49% to 96% of participants finding strips useful and wanting to use them again, has eight rows from seven studies; five give the percentage who would use strips again: Park et al. (ref. 52) Baltimore 2019, 123 participants, 49%, and Delaware 2019, 102, 74%; Sutherland (ref. 91) Sydney, Australia, 2021, 78, 96% if strips were free to access; Krieger (ref. 29) Rhode Island 2017, 93, 95%; and Klaire (ref. 92) Vancouver 2019, 218, 95%. The other three give median ratings out of 10 (12 participants), a statement that most had positive experiences, and mixed views. Appendix 1 identifies ref. 52 as Park et al. (2021, fentanyl test strip distribution in two Mid-Atlantic syringe services programmes), ref. 91 as Sutherland et al. (2021, take-home fentanyl test strips, a one-page item in a Drug and Alcohol Review supplement), ref. 29 as a 2018 conference abstract by Krieger on willingness to use strips among young adults, and ref. 92 as Klaire et al. (2022, take-home drug checking in British Columbia), also listed as ref. 66.

Overdose risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days at baseline, 414 people who had used strips against 312 who had not (the 726 in the analysed sample who used drugs in the past 30 days): composite score median 8.0 (quartiles 7.0–10.0) against 7.0 (5.0–8.0) and number of behaviours median 6.0 (5.0–7.0) against 5.0 (4.0–6.0), each P < .001 (both missing for 112); answering always: naloxone nearby 267 of 414 (64.5%) against 121 of 312 (38.8%), someone else present 53.4% against 43.3%, testing the strength of drugs 36.5% against 17.0% (never 14.7% against 53.8%), using slowly 33.1% against 19.9%, asking someone to check on them 27.3% against 9.3%, watching someone use the same drugs first 15.7% against 9.0%, and using by routes other than injection 32.4% against 41.5%. The table gives medians, not the means the article's text names. Editors' calculation: 267 of 414 is 64.49%, 64 in 100; 121 of 312 is 38.78%, 39 in 100.

The review's complete reference list identifies reference 63, the one study it cites for drug checking services being more likely to be used by people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months, suspected fentanyl exposure, injected in public, did sex work or had had a non-fatal overdose, as Beaulieu et al. (2020), on the effect of witnessing an overdose on the use of drug checking services among people who use illicit drugs in Vancouver, Canada (American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse 46:506–511); the primary study was not read.

tasks.extracted: Online Appendix A (added by the 2026 corrigendum): the treatment indicator marks, for each state and month, whether legal fentanyl test strips were available in a way the authors judged capable of a meaningful policy shock; for most jurisdictions the date is the statute's effective date as in the NPHL database (cited there as Davis et al., 2022), and for five the authors depart from it. Table A1, source date and date used: Alabama June 1, 2022, untreated through 2022 (enforcement and pharmacy uncertainty: an Alabama drug threat assessment from 2023 describing legalization as pending, and a pharmacist survey that Table A1 places in 2025, in which 25.2% believed strips were still illegal); Minnesota July 1, 2021, untreated (state law keeps cities' power to ban paraphernalia; two cities named); New Mexico May 18, 2022, untreated (distribution still an offence; implementing rules effective November 29, 2022); North Carolina 2019, treated from July 22, 2022, three years after enactment (a narrow statute; a March–May 2022 pharmacist survey found two pharmacies dispensing strips); District of Columbia April 11, 2019, treated from August 2019 (overlapping emergency, temporary and permanent laws; a local organization's August 2019 statement that the framework was complete as of May 2019). Virginia (July 1, 2019) and West Virginia (June 10, 2022) keep the source's dates after review, as do all states the appendix does not discuss. The authors write that reasonable researchers may reach different judgments. No results with the source's dates are reported, and the six jurisdictions shaded legal on the paper's map without a date (Alaska, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Vermont, Wyoming) are not mentioned.
